implementation_notes: ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent is the JVM's memo primitive with a real guarantee behind it: the whole method invocation is atomic and the mapping function is invoked exactly once per invocation when the key is absent, so a shared memo computes each key once even when many threads miss together. Three documented constraints shape the design - the mapping function must not modify the map during computation (a computation that detectably attempts a recursive update that would never complete throws IllegalStateException), other update operations on that bin may block while the function runs so it should be short, and null keys and values are not allowed, so a legitimate null result must be wrapped. This replaces the synchronized-map idiom that used to surround every read.
pitfalls: The mapping function must not modify the map: a recursive memo that recomputes through the same ConcurrentHashMap throws IllegalStateException instead of overflowing the stack.
Long computations inside computeIfAbsent block concurrent updates to the same bin, so a slow or blocking mapping function degrades the whole cache; keep the function short and side-effect free.
Null is not a legal value, so a function that can return null must be wrapped (Optional, a sentinel) or it will throw.
Mutable keys (or keys whose hashCode changes) make stored entries unreachable; the map is not rehashed when a key mutates.

variants.name: HashMap.computeIfAbsent for a single-owner memo
variants.implementation_notes: When the memo belongs to one thread - a parse, a batch job, an object that is provably confined - a plain HashMap with computeIfAbsent is the cheaper and more forgiving form: the method's own documentation names constructing a memoized result as its most common usage, there is no bin locking, null values are permitted (a key mapped to null counts as absent), and recursion through the same map is an ordinary computation rather than an error. It replaces the get/put pair of pre-Java-8 code with one call and reads better than a manual containsKey guard. The class documentation is equally explicit about the limit: HashMap is not synchronized, so concurrent structural access must be synchronised externally - the ConcurrentHashMap above is justified the moment the memo is actually shared, because here a shared memo is a data race rather than an optimisation.
pitfalls: HashMap is not synchronized: sharing this memo across threads is a data race, even though every individual call looks atomic.

computeIfAbsent on a HashMap still forbids structural modification of the map from inside the mapping function, and detection is only best-effort: the documented outcome is a ConcurrentModificationException when it is detected, corrupted state when it is not.
Unbounded and never evicting: for request-derived keys this is a memory leak, not a cache.
Keys must be immutable and must implement equals/hashCode consistently with the caller's idea of the same inputs, or equal arguments land in different entries.

variants.name: Guava Suppliers.memoize for a nullary value
variants.implementation_notes: For the argument-free case Guava supplies the whole pattern as one call: Suppliers.memoize caches the instance retrieved by the first get() and returns it thereafter, is thread-safe, and invokes the delegate at most once unless the delegate throws - a thrown exception is not memoized, so the next call retries. memoizeWithExpiration adds a time-to-live for values that must be refreshed, which is the smallest honest step from memoization towards a real cache. It does not key on arguments, so it complements rather than replaces the map-based variants; when the supplier itself is expensive and the JVM is long-lived, the memoized supplier is still a permanent retention point.
pitfalls: Exceptions are not memoized by design: a supplier that fails will be retried on every call, which can turn a broken dependency into repeated slow failures.
A memoized supplier never releases its value, so wiring one per request or per object creates retention that outlives the thing it was built for.
No key, therefore no argument-keyed memoization; reaching for memoizeWithExpiration to build a cache is a sign that cache-aside with a real cache is the better tool.
Serialisation does not carry the cached value, and a deserialised supplier recomputes on first use.
